summary: Psalm 44 begins by remembering that God, not Israel's weapons, gave the ancestors victory and land. The poem then turns sharply: the community says God has rejected, scattered, and shamed them even though they have not forgotten him or turned to another god. It ends as an urgent plea for God to wake, help, and redeem them for his loving kindness' sake.
whyItMatters: This chapter gives the Psalter a communal lament in which remembered rescue and present defeat stand side by side. It shows that the book makes room for protest when suffering does not seem to match the community's claimed faithfulness.

context.author: The heading associates the psalm with the sons of Korah; Psalms as a whole is a many-author anthology, and headings may indicate authorship, association, dedication, or collection.
context.audience: Israel's worshiping and instructed community, with later Jewish and Christian communities also receiving the Psalms as prayer and Scripture.
context.date: The Psalms preserve material from different periods, from the monarchy through the postexilic period; one date for the whole collection would be misleading.
context.setting: Book II of the Psalter, where Korahite and other collections appear; this psalm speaks from communal military defeat, shame, and scattering among nations.
context.literaryForm: Hebrew poetic communal lament, using memory, accusation, protest of loyalty, and petition.

outline.heading: Inherited memory of God's past help
outline.note: The speakers recall what their fathers told them: God drove out nations, planted the ancestors, and gave possession by his own hand rather than by their sword.

outline.heading: Confidence in God, not weapons
outline.note: The community calls God king, asks for victories, rejects trust in bow or sword, and boasts in God's name.

outline.heading: Present defeat and public shame
outline.note: The poem turns to the current crisis: rejection, retreat, plunder, scattering, ridicule, dishonor, and verbal abuse.

outline.heading: Claim of continued loyalty
outline.note: The speakers say they have not forgotten God, broken covenant, turned back, or reached toward a strange god, while insisting God knows the heart.

outline.heading: Urgent appeal for rescue
outline.note: The psalm ends by asking God to wake, stop hiding his face, see their affliction, and redeem them for his loving kindness' sake.

keyVerses.text: For they didn’t get the land in possession by their own sword, neither did their own arm save them; but your right hand, your arm, and the light of your face, because you were favorable to them.
keyVerses.why: This verse states the chapter's memory of the past: the ancestors' security came from God, not from their own military strength.

keyVerses.text: But now you rejected us, and brought us to dishonor, and don’t go out with our armies.
keyVerses.why: This is the sharp turn from remembered favor to present defeat. The lament directly addresses God as the one whose absence is felt in battle.

keyVerses.text: All this has come on us, yet we haven’t forgotten you. We haven’t been false to your covenant.
keyVerses.why: This anchors the psalm's difficult claim: the community does not present its suffering as the obvious result of abandoning God.

keyVerses.text: Rise up to help us. Redeem us for your loving kindness’ sake.
keyVerses.why: The final verse gathers the whole poem into a direct plea for rescue grounded in God's loving kindness.

questions.question: Who is speaking in Psalm 44?
questions.answer: The psalm mostly speaks in the voice of a community using “we,” “us,” and “our.” Even when verse 4 says “my King” and verse 15 says “my dishonor,” the poem remains centered on shared memory, shared defeat, and shared appeal. The heading links it with the sons of Korah, but the chapter itself presents a communal lament.

questions.question: What does the opening say the fathers passed down?
questions.answer: They passed down memory of what God had done “in the days of old.” The remembered work is the settling of the ancestors: God drove out nations, planted them, and gave possession by his hand and favor. The point is not a full history lesson, but a confession that the earlier victory belonged to God.

questions.question: Why does the psalm reject trust in bow and sword?
questions.answer: The speakers say their ancestors did not gain the land by their own sword, and they now say, “I will not trust in my bow.” Bow and sword are real weapons in the poem, but they are not treated as ultimate sources of rescue. The psalm contrasts military means with dependence on God.

questions.question: What changed at verse 9?
questions.answer: Verse 9 begins with “But now,” marking the major turn in the chapter. After remembering God as the giver of victory, the community says God has rejected them, brought dishonor, and no longer goes out with their armies. The poem holds the past and present in unresolved tension.

questions.question: Is the community admitting guilt for its suffering?
questions.answer: No. The speakers explicitly say they have not forgotten God, have not been false to the covenant, and have not spread out their hands to a strange god. Readers may debate how to evaluate that claim, but the chapter itself presents the suffering as a problem precisely because the community claims continued loyalty.

questions.question: What does “Selah” mean here?
questions.answer: “Selah” appears at the end of verse 8 after the community says it will give thanks to God's name forever. It is an uncertain musical or performance marker whose exact instruction is no longer known. A first-time reader can notice it as a performance marker without pretending to know the original performance detail.

questions.question: Why does the psalm say, “Wake up! Why do you sleep, Lord?”
questions.answer: The line speaks to God in the language of urgent complaint, as if God's help is absent or delayed. It does not explain God literally sleeping; it portrays how the crisis feels to the speakers. The next lines clarify the request: arise, stop rejecting, stop hiding your face, and remember their affliction.

questions.question: What is meant by being “regarded as sheep for the slaughter”?
questions.answer: The image describes vulnerability and repeated killing: “for your sake we are killed all day long.” It echoes the earlier image of being made “like sheep for food.” Later Christian readers connect this verse with suffering for God, but in this chapter it first belongs to the community's lament over danger and defeat.

questions.question: How does the psalm end?
questions.answer: It ends without reporting a rescue. The final posture is petition: the speakers say their soul is bowed down and their body clings to the earth, then ask God to rise up, help, and redeem them. The last reason given is God's “loving kindness,” not the community's ability to fix the crisis.

glossary.def: A group named in the heading of this psalm. In the Psalms, such headings can mark association, collection, performance, dedication, or authorship, and should be read carefully rather than as a modern byline.
A preserved performance term in verse 8. Its exact ancient instruction is uncertain, so it is best treated as a signal within the poem rather than translated into a confident command.
The binding relationship named in verse 17 when the speakers say they have not been false to God. In this chapter, it matters because the community claims loyalty while suffering defeat.
The phrase in verse 20 for another deity. The speakers deny turning toward one, strengthening their claim that their suffering is not because they abandoned God.
The reason named in the final plea for redemption. The psalm asks God to act because of this faithful mercy, even though no rescue is narrated within the chapter.
